=============== #1793
redact_observed_value: scalar observed_value fails OPEN (not closed) when tested_column can't be resolved
---
## Context

Found during review of #1791 (the #1772 fix), which added a new caller of `run_service.redact_observed_value` (`incident_evidence.py::_failing_result_layer`). The defect itself predates that PR — it's in the shared function every results-facing surface calls (REST `runs.py::_result_read`, MCP `_run_results_payload`, `alerting/builder.py::build_run_report`, and now `incident_evidence.py`) — but a new caller means a new surface newly exercises it, and it's worth its own fix rather than folding into an already-large security PR.

## The problem

`run_service.py:1068-1079`:

```python
if isinstance(raw_observed_value, list):
    show = tested_column is not None and not _known_sensitive(...)   # unknown column -> HIDE (fail CLOSED)
    ...
show = tested_column is None or not _known_sensitive(...)             # scalar: unknown column -> SHOW (fail OPEN)
```

For **list**-shaped observed values, an unresolved `tested_column` fails closed (redacts). For **scalar** values — the exact case the #1772 fix's own docstring cites as the whole reason redaction is needed (`expect_column_min/max_to_be_between`-style rules carrying a literal warehouse cell) — an unresolved `tested_column` fails **open**, and due to `or` short-circuiting, `_known_sensitive` (including its value-shape heuristic, e.g. detecting an email-looking string) is **never even called**.

## Failure scenario

`tested_column` comes from `historical_check_context`, which falls back to `check.config.get("column")` when no `CheckVersion` history exists. Any check whose config genuinely has no `"column"` key — custom-SQL checks (ADR 0019) have no single derivable column — reaches this code with `tested_column=None`. A scalar `observed_value` is then shown with **zero** screening: not tag-based, not policy-based, not value-shape-based — even on an asset carrying a hard-floor `sensitive` warehouse tag on the column the custom SQL happens to select. This is live today on every existing caller (REST results, MCP results, alert delivery), not just the new incident-evidence path.

## Fix

Make the scalar branch symmetric with the list branch: when `tested_column is None`, fail closed (redact) rather than show, unless there's a principled reason scalars should default-open that lists don't (if so, document it explicitly — right now the asymmetry reads as accidental, not a decision). Needs a regression test with a custom-SQL-shaped check (no `config.column`) and a scalar observed_value that should be masked under a PII policy/tag but currently isn't. Touches all four callers, so verify each doesn't rely on the current fail-open behavior for something legitimate (e.g. a non-sensitive scalar aggregate check with a deliberately absent column) before flipping the default.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1795
data-subject-rights export/erase never reach incidents.evidence
---
## Context

Found during a docs staleness audit ahead of the 2026-09-01 deploy, cross-checking `docs/site/compliance/dpia-input-sheet.md` and `docs/site/compliance/data-subject-rights-runbook.md` against the actual code.

## The gap

`backend/app/services/data_subject_requests.py` (`export_matching_results` / `erase_matching_results`, backing `POST /api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/{export,erase}`) scans and scrubs only `results.sample_failures` and `results.observed_value`. It never references `incidents`/`Incident`/`evidence` at all.

Since #1772/#1791, `Incident.evidence.failing_result.observed_value` is a third, distinct, persisted location that can carry the same kind of literal warehouse cell value as `results.observed_value` — captured once when an incident opens or gets a fresh occurrence, and (unlike `results`) **not covered by the retention purge sweep** either (grepped `backend/app/services/retention.py` and `worker/tasks.py` — no hits for "evidence").

## Failure scenario

A controller receives a GDPR Art 17 erasure request for `column=email, value=alice@example.com`. An admin runs `POST /api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/erase`, gets back `{matched_count: 1, erased_count: 1}`, and reasonably tells the data subject their data is erased. If that same value also landed in an incident's evidence snapshot (a suite with a check on the `email` column that once failed), the value is **still there**, readable via `get_incident` (REST/MCP) indefinitely — the erasure response gives no signal that this happened.

## Current mitigation

Docs now disclose this explicitly rather than overclaim coverage (`data-subject-rights-runbook.md` §0 and §5, `dpia-input-sheet.md`'s Class 1 table) — this issue is the code-side fix that closes the gap the docs describe.

## Fix

Extend `export_matching_results`/`erase_matching_results` to also scan `Incident.evidence` for workspace incidents, using the same `(column, value)` match logic already applied to `results.observed_value`'s shapes, and scrub in place the same way `redact_stale_incident_evidence.py` (#1772) already knows how to rewrite `Incident.evidence` in place. Update `matched_count`/`erased_count` to include incident hits, and extend the §4 exercise steps + the runbook's disclosed limits once fixed.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1792
incident_evidence: N+1 historical_check_context query per failing result in a run
---
## Context

Filed during review of #1791 (the #1772 fix). Two independent review passes (an efficiency/reuse pass and a correctness pass) both flagged the same shape.

## The problem

`incident_evidence.py::_failing_result_layer` calls:

```python
tested_column, _expectation_type = run_service.historical_check_context(
    session, [result], {check.id: check}
).get(result.id, (None, None))
```

once **per failing result**, invoked from `incident_service.py::_sync_incidents_for_run`'s per-result loop (via `open_or_attach_incident` → `build_evidence`). `historical_check_context` unconditionally issues a `CheckVersion` query when `check_ids` is non-empty, so a run with N failing checks issues N separate `CheckVersion` queries instead of one batched `IN (...)` query.

Every other call site in the codebase resolves this **once per run**, over the whole `results` list, then does O(1) dict lookups:
- `backend/app/api/v1/runs.py:309` — `context = svc.historical_check_context(db, results, checks)` once, then `context.get(r.id, ...)` per result.
- `backend/app/mcp/server.py` — same shape.

`_failing_result_layer` also re-derives `suite` (`session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)`) and `tags` per call, where every sibling site resolves these once at the top of the enclosing function and threads them down as parameters.

## Impact

Bounded by the number of failing checks in one run (typically small), so not a scaling emergency, but a real avoidable cost that grows with the size of a table-wide outage (exactly the case `_sibling_checks_layer` exists to describe — many checks failing together).

## Fix

Lift `historical_check_context` (and `suite`/`tested_column`) resolution to `_sync_incidents_for_run`, batched once over all failing results in the run, and thread the resolved values down through `open_or_attach_incident` → `build_evidence` → `_failing_result_layer`, matching the pattern already established in `runs.py`/`mcp/server.py`.

## Also noted, lower priority

`incident_evidence.py`'s new redaction call path has no regression test exercising an exception thrown *inside* `_failing_result_layer`'s redaction branch (the existing `test_raising_layer_degrades_to_none_other_layers_intact` monkeypatches a different layer). No live producer currently writes a non-dict `observed_value`, so this is speculative — worth a test if this area is touched again.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1729
bug(core): jsonsafe.sanitize_json sanitizes dict values but not dict keys — latent JSONB-insert crash on a bytes/Decimal key
---
## Summary
`backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py:41` recurses into dict **values** only:
```python
if isinstance(value, dict):
    return {key: sanitize_json(item) for key, item in value.items()}
```
The **key** is passed through untouched. A `bytes`/`Decimal`/numpy value used as a dict key — e.g. a `{column_value: count}` metric over a BINARY or NUMERIC column — reaches the JSONB encoder raw and crashes the whole result's insert. This is the exact #1273/#1719 class the sanitizer's own `Decimal` and (new) `bytes` branches fix for values; the new bytes branch makes the asymmetry sharper. `memoryview` (psycopg-style BYTEA) is likewise unhandled — verified likely-benign for the current datasource drivers (Snowflake → bytearray, databricks-sql → bytes), so listing for completeness.

## Fix

=============== #1732
security(connections): update_connection accepts secret="" as 'credential re-supplied' at the service layer — blank-credential + redirect-guard bypass rests on a single API-model check
---
## Summary
`backend/app/services/connection_service.py` treats `secret is not None` as 'rotate' (`:576`) and `_reject_uncredentialed_redirect` treats `supplied_secret is not None` as 'credential re-supplied' (`:137`). An empty string therefore both **passes the #1401/#1403 redirect guard** and **blanks the stored credential**.

Today this is blocked only at the API model (`backend/app/api/v1/connections.py:48-51`, `secret: … min_length=1`) — the #1403 fix. The service function itself has no floor, so the invariant rests on a single layer; any future non-HTTP caller (an internal task, a new router) reaching `update_connection` directly reintroduces the blank-credential + destination-redirect path.

## Fix
Reject empty `secret`/`catalog_secret` in the service, not just the schema — defense-in-depth at the layer that actually enforces the invariant. (`reauth` has carried `min_length=1` since it shipped; create/update should match at the service boundary.)

Found in a full-codebase QA auth/secrets audit.
--- COMMENTS:
## Reproduction
Service-layer (the API model `min_length=1` at `connections.py:48-51` is the ONLY thing blocking this today):
```python
# a caller reaching the service directly (internal task / future router), bypassing the schema
connection_service.update_connection(
    session, connection_id=<id>, actor=<admin>,
    config={... 'account': 'NEW-HOST' ...},   # a destination move
    secret='',                                 # empty string
    secret_store=store)
# _reject_uncredentialed_redirect sees supplied_secret is not None -> redirect guard PASSES (:137)
# update_connection sees secret is not None -> rotates -> stores '' -> credential BLANKED (:576)
```
Via HTTP this is refused (422, min_length=1). The invariant rests on that single layer; the service has no floor. Fix = reject empty secret/catalog_secret in the service.
=============== #1787
check_service.validate_monitor_check echoes an unbounded raw config dict in CheckConfigInvalidError.detail
---
## Summary
`check_service.py:325`:
```python
except MonitorConfigError as exc:
    raise CheckConfigInvalidError(str(exc), detail={"kind": kind, "config": config}) from exc
```
embeds the **entire, unbounded, caller-supplied `config` dict** in `detail` whenever a monitor-kind check (freshness/volume) fails identifier validation (`datasources/monitors.py`'s `_ident`, which itself echoes `name!r` with no length cap — unlike `check_service.py`'s own `_ERROR_ECHO_MAX_CHARS`/`_reject_oversized_config` convention, wired into `validate_expectation_check`/`validate_comparison_check` but not `validate_monitor_check`).

## Where this reaches an untrusted caller
- Directly: any REST route creating/updating a monitor-kind check surfaces `DataQError.detail` verbatim via the global exception handler's error envelope (`core/errors.py`), so a user-submitted oversized `config` value is echoed straight back in the 4xx response.
- Indirectly, via LLM check-suggestions: `llm_checksuggest._validate_freshness_suggestion` routes a model-proposed freshness suggestion through this same `validate_monitor_check` path. #1786 added a size cap (`_DETAIL_MAX_CHARS = 4096`, `llm_service.py`) at the point `execute_invocation` persists `DataQError.detail` into `llm_invocations.response`, so the *persisted* row is now bounded — but the unbounded echo at the source (`check_service.py`/`monitors.py`) is still real and would still affect the synchronous REST path for human-authored checks, which has no equivalent size guard.

## Fix
Apply the same `_ERROR_ECHO_MAX_CHARS`/`_reject_oversized_config` (or equivalent) discipline `validate_expectation_check`/`validate_comparison_check` already use, to `validate_monitor_check` and `_ident`.

Found during `/code-review`'s cross-file trace on PR #1786 (#1781 — execute_invocation persisting DataQError.detail).

=============== #1717
perf(llm): llm_invocations has no index on status — the #1644 reaper and poller both do unindexed sequential scans
---
From the /code-review on #1716 (the llm_invocations reaper).

**Problem:** \`llm_invocations\` (backend/app/db/models.py) has only \`ix_llm_invocations_requested_by\`. The #1644 reaper's beat task queries \`WHERE status = 'pending'\`/\`WHERE status = 'running'\` every 5 minutes, and the UI poll path likely filters similarly — both are unindexed sequential scans, growing linearly with the table's full history since the row is deliberately retained forever (the model's own docstring: "safe to retain like other operational history").

**Not a bug today:** the table is small (the LLM track shipped in W3). Filed so it doesn't get lost as invocation volume grows.

**Fix:** a partial index on \`status\` covering the two non-terminal values, e.g. \`CREATE INDEX ix_llm_invocations_status_open ON llm_invocations (status) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'running')\` — small, append-mostly, backward-compatible (CONTRIBUTING migration rules).

**Explicitly not in scope:** a retention/purge sweep — \`llm_invocations\` is the G4 audit/cost record and is retained by design, unlike \`runs\`/\`results\`.

=============== #1790
reliability(worker): verify/set explicit Celery concurrency — perf-baseline.md claims concurrency=4 but no deploy config sets it
---
## Summary
`docs/site/perf-baseline.md` describes its "production parity" measurement rig as `worker at 1 CPU / 2 GiB / celery --concurrency=4 (matched to the deployed worker)`. But none of the actual worker startup commands — `docker-compose.yml`, `docker-compose.ghcr.yml`, `deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf`, `deploy/terraform/aws/ecs.tf` — pass an explicit `--concurrency`/`-c` flag. The worker runs whatever Celery's prefork pool defaults to (`os.cpu_count()`), which under a cgroup-limited 1-vCPU container is famously unreliable — it can resolve to the host's full core count rather than the container's actual allocation, or in some runtimes correctly report 1.

## Why this matters
Found while reviewing #1789 (dedicated Celery queue for `llm_invoke`, closing #1726 Part A). That fix's own doc comment originally claimed queue separation means "a long run_suite backlog no longer starves llm_invoke dispatches" — corrected during review to be precise: queue separation only prevents FIFO blocking at the *dispatch/fetch* level (a queued `run_suite` message no longer blocks `llm_invoke` from being pulled off the broker). It does **not** add an execution slot — if the worker's actual concurrency is 1 (plausible under the unverified cgroup-default behavior above), a single already-*running* long suite (this deployment class has 1M-200M-row UC perf suites) can still occupy the worker's only active slot for its full duration, and an `llm_invoke` task fetched from the now-separate queue still has nowhere to run until that slot frees up.

## Ask
1. Determine the ACTUAL effective concurrency on both deployed workers (live check — `celery -A backend.app.worker.celery_app inspect stats` or equivalent, per this project's own "only a live run is evidence for anything crossing this class of boundary" rule; don't infer from `os.cpu_count()` semantics).
2. If it's not the `perf-baseline.md`-documented 4 (or whatever the actual production-representative capacity target is), either set an explicit `--concurrency` flag on all four worker-launch locations, or correct `perf-baseline.md` to describe reality instead of an aspirational/wrong number.
3. Once concurrency is verified/fixed, consider whether `llm_invoke` warrants a reserved execution slot (not just a separate queue) so a long suite run can never fully starve it — a bigger architectural question, out of scope for this issue but worth recording as the next question if concurrency turns out to be the binding constraint.

Not a regression from #1789 — a pre-existing gap the review surfaced.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1731
security(auth): email-enumeration timing side-channel — OTP request floor is a minimum, and the eligible path does a synchronous SMTP send before it
---
## Summary
`request_otp` (`backend/app/api/v1/auth_otp.py:79-104`) pads responses to `auth_otp_request_min_seconds` (default 1.0s), but that is a **minimum**, not a maximum. The eligible branch runs `is_signup_eligible` → per-email quota → DB writes → a **synchronous** `mailer.send_code()` (real SMTP round-trip) *before* the floor is applied; ineligible/throttled branches return fast and are padded to the same floor.

When a real relay (e.g. SES) pushes the eligible path's own work past ~1s, an allow-listed address produces a measurably longer tail than a non-member — revealing which addresses are workspace members. The code comment ("Only a real mail-transport failure differs") is optimistic: a slow-but-successful send also differs.

## Impact / severity
Low and deployment-dependent (floor vs. relay latency); Mailpit-local won't exhibit it. Membership enumeration only, not credential compromise.

## Fix
Send mail out-of-band (queue) so the response time is independent of transport latency, or measure-and-cap the send inside the floored region.

Found in a full-codebase QA auth surface audit (surface otherwise verified clean — no blocker/major).
--- COMMENTS:
## How to observe (statistical — deployment-dependent, not a single-shot repro)
Requires a real SMTP relay whose send latency can exceed the 1.0s floor (Mailpit-local will NOT exhibit it):
1. Configure a live relay (e.g. SES) for OTP.
2. Time `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` for (a) an allow-listed/member address vs (b) a non-member address, N≥100 samples each.
3. Observed: (a)'s tail exceeds (b)'s whenever the synchronous `mailer.send_code()` pushes the eligible path past the floor — the floor pads (b) up to ~1.0s but cannot pad (a) *down*. The delta reveals membership.

The mechanism is confirmed by inspection: the floor (`_hold_until_floor`) is a minimum applied *after* the eligible branch's synchronous SMTP send (`auth_otp.py:79-104`, `otp_service.py:230-272`). Severity is low/deployment-dependent, hence P3.
=============== #1693
feat(admin): in-app workspace membership — admins add/remove members without touching env config (ADR 0043)
---
## Problem
An admin cannot add (or remove) a workspace member in DataQ. A user row is created lazily on first successful sign-in, and who may sign in is governed entirely by DEPLOYMENT ENV CONFIG: `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS`/`_DOMAINS` (generic OIDC, #1386), `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS`/`_DOMAINS` (OTP — the allowlist IS the member list), tenant membership (Azure AD). "Add Priya" = edit env vars + restart/redeploy + wait for her first login before a role can even be assigned. The Admin page manages roles of people already inside, not who gets in.

**Revocation is also inconsistent per door (verified 2026-08-29):** OIDC allowlist revokes per-request; OTP re-checks eligibility only at code request/redemption — a live `dq_sess_` session survives until TTL; a PAT never re-checks membership at all.

## Scope (user-directed 2026-08-29)
- **IdP account creation stays a prerequisite — we do NOT touch the IdP.** DataQ governs only its own door; the UI states this plainly for OIDC/Azure modes.
- New `workspace_members` table: normalized unique email, `initial_role`, invited_by, created_at. Admin CRUD at `/admin/members` (audited, G1).
- **Enforcement semantics:** DB table EMPTY → exactly today's behavior per mode (zero-migration-risk default). Table NON-EMPTY → union(env allowlist, DB rows) is the membership list, enforced per-request at the shared resolver choke points: `_upsert_user` (OIDC/Azure/MCP), `session_service.resolve_token` (OTP sessions), `api_key_service.resolve_token` (PATs, REST + MCP), `otp_service.is_signup_eligible` (both call sites). Dev-bypass exempt. This CLOSES the per-door revocation inconsistency — removal bites on the next request regardless of credential kind.
- Env allowlists demote to **bootstrap seed + break-glass, grant-only** — the ADR 0033 `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` pattern exactly.
- **Lockout guards:** the FIRST db row write auto-imports all existing users as members in the same transaction (turning enforcement on can never evict current users); removing the membership of the last admin-role user refuses (FOR UPDATE, mirroring #1400's last-admin guard); self-removal requires explicit confirm.
- **Pre-provisioned role:** `initial_role` seeds the user row at first sign-in (new-row branch only — the conflict branch stays promote-only per ADR 0033; the Members role editor remains authoritative after that).
- Frontend: Members & Access panel gains Add member (email + role), a pending-invites view (member rows with no user row yet), remove with the enforcement-state warning.

## Out of scope (recorded)
OTP invite emails (the code-request email already reaches them); IdP user provisioning; user deactivation/offboarding-transfer (#412's write pass); multi-workspace.

## Verification bar
Every choke point mutation-verified (a gate whose removal leaves the sweep green is not a gate — the #1424-class trap); the auto-import transactionality proven on real Postgres; revocation proven per credential kind (live session, live PAT) not just per door; superuser/commit test-blindness lessons apply (#1621).

Refs: #1386, ADR 0032/0033, #1400, #412 (the wider admin write pass), the 2026-08-29 admin-UI design conversation.

## Findings (angle: simplification)

**1. `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py:59-60` — redundant `isinstance(key, str)` fast-path duplicates the `isinstance(sanitized, str)` check two lines later**
`_json_key` special-cases `str` keys before calling `sanitize_json`, but `sanitize_json(key)` is a no-op for strings anyway (falls through every branch and returns `value` unchanged), so the later `isinstance(sanitized, str)` branch already covers it correctly.
failure_scenario: two branches now do the same job for the common case (plain string keys, the overwhelming majority in practice), so a future editor "fixing" one string-handling path can easily forget the other exists and diverge them (e.g. adding stripping/normalization to one but not the other). Simpler form: drop the fast-path entirely — `sanitized = sanitize_json(key); return sanitized if isinstance(sanitized, str) else (json.dumps(sanitized) if sanitized is None or isinstance(sanitized, (bool, int, float)) else str(sanitized))`. (The fast-path is a micro-optimization avoiding one function call for str keys — not worth the duplicate logic path.)

**2. `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py:64-65` — three-way branch is really `json.dumps` doing the exact same thing `sanitize_json`+the docstring already promise**
The function reimplements `json.dumps`'s scalar-key stringification rule by hand (`None`/`bool`/`int`/`float` → `json.dumps(sanitized)`) instead of just relying on `json.dumps({key: 0})` behavior once, or dumping the single value.
failure_scenario: if `json.dumps`'s key-stringification rules ever need to change (e.g. Python changes `True`→`"true"` casing, unlikely but illustrative), there are now two independent code paths (this branch and any place value-serialization is tested) that must be kept in sync manually. def is_sensitive(
    name: str,
    sampled_values: Sequence[object] | None = None,
    *,
    value_signal_summary: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> bool:
    """Whether a column is **affirmatively** PII — a person/sensitive name token or a
    directly-sensitive value signal (emails, encoded blobs) — as opposed to the
    conservative *default* mask.
    """
    return (
        _name_signal(name) is ColumnClass.PII
        or _value_signal(list(sampled_values or []), value_signal_summary=value_signal_summary)
        is ColumnClass.PII
    )

def build_run_report(session: Session, run: Run) -> RunReport:
    """Build the redacted, GX-agnostic report for a terminal ``run``."""
    suite = session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    connection = session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id) if suite is not None else None
    asset = run_service.resolve_asset(session, suite, run)
    owner = _resolve_owner(session, asset, suite)
    checks = {c.id: c for c in session.scalars(select(Check).where(Check.suite_id == run.suite_id))}
    # The warehouse's own column classifications (G3, #433) — the same governance floor the REST and
    # MCP read paths apply.
    tags = asset.column_tags if asset is not None else None
    results: list[Result] = run_service.list_results(session, run.id)

    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    check_reports: list[CheckReport] = []
    for result in results:
        counts[result.status] = counts.get(result.status, 0) + 1
        check = checks.get(result.check_id)
        check_reports.append(
            CheckReport(
                check_name=check.name if check is not None else "(deleted check)",
                expectation_type=check.expectation_type if check is not None else "",
                status=result.status,
                metric_value=(
                    float(result.metric_value) if result.metric_value is not None else None
                ),
                observed_value=run_service.redact_observed_value(
                    result.observed_value,
                    tested_column=(check.config.get("column") if check is not None else None),
                    expectation_type=(check.expectation_type if check is not None else None),
                    policy=suite.column_policy if suite is not None else None,
                    tags=tags,
                ),
                expected_value=result.expected_value,
                # Column-aware redaction (#415): the tested column's failing values
                # surface when non-PII; the suite policy + heuristics mask PII.
                sample_summary=run_service.redact_sample_failures(
                    result.sample_failures,
                    tested_column=(check.config.get("column") if check is not None else None),
                    policy=suite.column_policy if suite is not None else None,
                    tags=tags,
                ),
            )
        )

    has no way to know the list is one phase of thirty — so an incomplete run
    yields no checks at all and says why, rather than a confident report built
    from a fraction of the suite.

    **The G1 access event is written here, not at the two call sites** (#431). The
    reason is the same one this function is shared for: a second copy of the audit
    call is a second place to forget it, and the surface it protects — who read
    which failing rows — is one where a silent gap is indistinguishable from
    nobody having looked.
    """
    final = run.status in rollup.AGGREGATABLE_RUN_STATUSES
    results = run_service.list_results(session, run.id) if final else []
    checks = {c.id: c for c in session.scalars(select(Check).where(Check.suite_id == suite.id))}
    policy = suite.column_policy
    # The warehouse's own column classifications (G3, #433) — the governance floor
    # a suite policy cannot lift. Read from the cached map on the asset, never
    # from the warehouse: an MCP read must not open a datasource connection.
    # `None` means no opinion, which is what shipped before G3.
    tags = _asset_column_tags(session, suite, run)
    # Per-RESULT (tested_column, expectation_type) as of when each result was
    # written (#1489) — not the check's current state, which is freely editable
    # after the fact and would silently re-label what old results show/audit.
    context = run_service.historical_check_context(session, results, checks)

    def _tested_column(result_id: uuid.UUID) -> str | None:
        return context.get(result_id, (None, None))[0]

    # Redact ONCE, here, and reuse below. An earlier version redacted every result
    # a second time purely to compute `exposed_ids` and then threw the result
    # away, so every MCP results read paid the redaction pass twice.
    rendered = [
        {
            "result_id": str(r.id),
            **_redacted_sample(r, _tested_column(r.id), policy, tags),
            "observed_value": run_service.redact_observed_value(
                r.observed_value,
                tested_column=_tested_column(r.id),
                expectation_type=context.get(r.id, (None, None))[1],
                policy=policy,
                tags=tags,
            ),
        }
        for r in results
    ]
    # `redaction` is the state the redactor computed for THIS read: `full` means
    # everything row-level was masked and `null` means there was no row-level
    # content at all, so neither exposed anything. `observed_value` is the OTHER

@router.get("/runs/{run_id}", response_model=RunDetailRead, summary="Get a run with its results")
def get_run(
    run_id: uuid.UUID,
    current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)],
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> RunDetailRead:
    run = svc.get_run(db, run_id)
    if run is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND, detail="run not found")
    # Gate on the run's suite: a caller who can't see the suite can't see its
    # runs (404 hides the run id too, matching the suite existence-hiding rule).
    suite = require_permission(db, run.suite_id, current_user.id, minimum="view")
    results = svc.list_results(db, run_id)
    checks = {c.id: c for c in db.scalars(select(Check).where(Check.suite_id == run.suite_id))}
    policy = suite.column_policy
    tags = _asset_column_tags(db, suite, run)
    # Per-RESULT (tested_column, expectation_type) as of when each result was written (#1489) — not
    # the check's current state.
    context = svc.historical_check_context(db, results, checks)
    # `Run` has no `results` relationship to validate a RunDetailRead from directly, so validate
    # the run fields (as RunRead), graft the data-quality outcome (#571 — else checks_total/passed
    # stay at the 0/0 default here), and attach the separately-fetched, redaction-gated results.
    outcome = svc.check_outcome_counts(db, [run.id]).get(run.id)
    expectation_types = {r.id: context.get(r.id, (None, None))[1] for r in results}
    reads = [
        _result_read(
            r,
            tested_column=context.get(r.id, (None, None))[0],
            expectation_type=expectation_types[r.id],
            policy=policy,
            tags=tags,
        )
        for r in results
    ]
    _audit_result_read(
        db, current_user, run=run, results=reads, expectation_types=expectation_types
    )
    return RunDetailRead(
        **RunRead.model_validate(run).model_copy(update=_outcome_update(outcome)).model_dump(),
        results=reads,
    )

## Summary

- `llm_invocations` had only `ix_llm_invocations_requested_by`. The #1644 reaper (`llm_service.reap_stuck_invocations`, beat task `reap_stuck_llm_invocations`) filters `status = 'pending'` and `status = 'running'` on every tick against a table that is retained forever by design (G4 audit/cost record), so both sweeps were sequential scans growing with the full history.
- Adds `ix_llm_invocations_status_open ON llm_invocations (status) WHERE status IN ('pending', 'running')` — in the SQLAlchemy model (`postgresql_where`) and as an additive Alembic migration `4a5f1e4d5daa` (down_revision `cadc40254699`; `alembic heads` shows exactly one head; id checked against the existing set). Partial, so it holds only the handful of in-flight rows.
- **Query/predicate alignment, checked against the real code:** the reaper never issues the `IN`-list itself — it runs two separate equality predicates (`status = 'pending' AND created_at < cutoff`, `status = 'running' AND started_at < cutoff`). A partial index is only usable when the planner can prove the query predicate implies the index predicate; each equality implies the `IN`-list, so the index is used for both — and a new test asserts that with `EXPLAIN` (under `enable_seqscan = off`, which cannot make an unprovable partial index eligible) rather than merely asserting the index exists. Mutation-checked: narrowing the predicate to `IN ('pending')` makes the `running` query fall back to a seq scan and the test fail.
- **One correction to the issue text:** the UI poller does *not* filter on status — `GET /llm/invocations/{id}` (`api/v1/llm.py`) reads by primary key, and the two conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND status = 'pending'` claim guards are PK-driven too. The reaper is the only non-PK read of this table; the index is sized and predicated for it.
- Migration-parity test (`test_migration_parity.py`) passes **unchanged**: `_literals()` extracts `{'pending', 'running'}` from both the model text and Postgres's `= ANY (ARRAY[...])` rewrite. The normalizer was not extended — an `IN` -> `NOT IN` flip would still be invisible, which is exactly #1605's scope; noted there (this PR makes that shape *present* in the model rather than hypothetical) rather than folded in.

## Context
Found by `/code-review` on #1801 (the #1793 fix).

## The gap
`backend/app/services/incident_service.py::redact_stale_evidence` — the REQUIRED post-deploy backfill (`backend/scripts/redact_stale_incident_evidence.py`, `deploy/README.md`) — passes `check.config.get("column")` and `check.expectation_type` from the check's **current** row. The live evidence builder (`incident_evidence._failing_result_layer`), REST `runs.py`, MCP `_run_results_payload` and (since #1801) `alerting/builder.py` all resolve the pair via `run_service.historical_check_context`, i.e. as of the result's own timestamp (#1489).

`PATCH /checks` allows changing `expectation_type` and `config.column`, so after an edit the backfill can classify a stored `Incident.evidence.failing_result.observed_value` differently from every other surface — and it rewrites the evidence **in place**, which is the only copy (no `Result` row is retained on the incident).

## Failure scenario
A check is edited from a column-less statistic type to a column-bearing type whose column is tagged PII after an incident opened. Re-running the backfill masks the stored count that the historical path would show (or the reverse). Irreversible.

## Fix

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3]
_LAUNCH_FILES = (
    "docker-compose.yml",

    "deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf",
    "deploy/terraform/aws/ecs.tf",
)
_WORKER_LINE = re.compile(r"^.*backend\\.app\\.worker\\.celery_app.*\\bworker\\b.*$", re.MULTILINE)


def _worker_commands(path: str) -> list[str]:
    text = (_ROOT / path).read_text()
    # Terraform spells the command as a JSON-ish array; normalise both shapes to one string.
    return [re.sub(r'[",\\[\\]]', " ", m.group(0)) for m in _WORKER_LINE.finditer(text)]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("path", _LAUNCH_FILES)
def test_every_worker_launch_pins_queues_and_concurrency(path: str) -> None:
    """Celery's prefork default is the HOST's core count, not the container's — the two
    reference deployments ran 4 and 2 on identical 1-vCPU tasks until it was pinned. A
    worker that omits the `llm` queue silently never consumes it.
    """
    commands = _worker_commands(path)
    assert commands, f"{path}: no worker launch command found"
    for command in commands:
        assert "celery,llm" in command, f"{path}: {command.strip()}"
        assert "--concurrency=4" in command, f"{path}: {command.strip()}"
''')
print("written")
EOF

Found by `/code-review` on #1810 (the #1790 fix, which pins Celery concurrency to 4 — the value Azure already ran by accident and `perf-baseline.md` measured with).

## The gap
`docs/site/perf-baseline.md` measured **single-run** worker peaks of ~1.2 GiB (CSV 1M) to ~1.7 GiB (UC 1M) under the 1 CPU / 2 GiB rig. With 4 prefork children, two overlapping large suites (a schedule collision, or a manual run beside a scheduled one) can push task RSS past the 2048 MiB hard limit. ECS/ACA then OOM-kill the **whole container**, which includes the embedded beat (`worker -B`) — every periodic task stops silently, the #405 class. `worker_max_memory_per_child_kb` recycles a child *between* tasks; it does not bound concurrent peaks.

This predates #1810 on Azure (it ran 4 already) and was masked on AWS only because the unpinned default happened to be 2.

## Options (decide in W6 perf)
1. Size memory to concurrency: 4 GiB worker tasks on both clouds (cost).
2. Lower concurrency to 2 and re-baseline (`perf-baseline.md` rig changes).
3. Keep 4 but add a per-task memory guard / admission control for sampled-vs-full scans (`ScanTooLargeError` already exists for the read side; a worker-level budget does not).
4. Split beat out of the worker container so an OOM can never take the scheduler down with it.

Whatever is chosen, record the concurrent-peak measurement, not just the single-run one.

Refs: #1790, #1810, #1393 (scale baseline), #405.

def find_matching_results(session: Session, *, column: str, value: str) -> list[MatchedResult]:
    """Workspace-wide scan for results whose captured sample/observed data names
    `column` = `value` for a subject's warehouse row. Read-only — the access/export
    half of the subject-rights machinery (GDPR Art 15/20).
    """
    rows = session.execute(_candidate_query()).all()
    # The tested column as of WHEN each result was written (#1489's fix, reused
    # here): the check's config can change after the fact, and matching on its
    # CURRENT column would silently miss a subject whose data was captured under
    # an earlier column name.
    context = historical_check_context(
        session,
        [result for result, _run, _suite, _check in rows],
        {check.id: check for _result, _run, _suite, check in rows},
    )
    matched: list[MatchedResult] = []
    for result, run, suite, check in rows:
        tested_column, _expectation_type = context.get(result.id, (None, None))
        hit_sample = _sample_matches(result.sample_failures, column=column, value=value)
        hit_observed = _observed_matches(
            result.observed_value, column=column, value=value, tested_column=tested_column
        )
        if not (hit_sample or hit_observed):
            continue
        kinds = tuple(
            k
            for k, hit in (("sample_failures", hit_sample), ("observed_value", hit_observed))
            if hit
        )
        matched.append(
            MatchedResult(
                result_id=result.id,
                run_id=run.id,
                suite_id=suite.id,
                suite_name=suite.name,
                check_id=check.id,
                check_name=check.name,
                created_at=result.created_at,
                matched_in=kinds,
                sample_failures=result.sample_failures,
                observed_value=result.observed_value,
                tested_column=tested_column,
            )
        )
    return matched


@dataclass
class ErasureSummary:
    #: Every result that matched the (column, value) pair, whether or not
    #: scrubbing actually changed it.
    matched_result_ids: list[UUID]
    erased_count: int


def erase_matching_results(session: Session, *, column: str, value: str) -> ErasureSummary:
    """On-demand erasure (GDPR Art 17 / CCPA delete): removes the matching
    row/cell from `sample_failures` and `observed_value` on every matched result,
    leaving the rest of each result's captured sample intact. Caller is
    responsible for the audit_events row and the commit (mirrors how other admin
    mutations in `admin_service` compose with the router).
    """
    matched = find_matching_results(session, column=column, value=value)
    erased_ids: list[UUID] = []
    for m in matched:
        result = session.get(Result, m.result_id)
        assert result is not None  # loaded in the same transaction, moments ago
        changed = False
        if result.sample_failures:
            scrubbed, sample_changed = _scrub_sample(
                result.sample_failures, column=column, value=value
            )
            if sample_changed:
                result.sample_failures = scrubbed
                changed = True
        if result.observed_value:
            scrubbed_obs, obs_changed = _scrub_observed(
                result.observed_value, column=column, value=value, tested_column=m.tested_column
            )
            if obs_changed:
                result.observed_value = scrubbed_obs
                changed = True
        if changed:
            erased_ids.append(m.result_id)
    return ErasureSummary(
        matched_result_ids=[m.result_id for m in matched], erased_count=len(erased_ids)
    )

class DataSubjectExportResponse(ApiModel):
    column: str
    value: str

@router.post(
    "/data-subject-requests/export",
    response_model=DataSubjectExportResponse,
    summary="Export a data subject's captured sample data (admin only, GDPR Art 15/20)",
)
def export_data_subject(
    payload: DataSubjectRequest,
    current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(require_workspace_admin)],
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> DataSubjectExportResponse:
    """Workspace-wide export of every captured sample cell naming
    `column` = `value` — the access/portability half of the subject-rights
    machinery. Returns unredacted data by design (see `DataSubjectMatch`), so this
    is deliberately Admin-only, same tier as a connection credential.
    """
    matches = data_subject_requests.find_matching_results(
        db, column=payload.column, value=payload.value
    )
    audit_service.record_access(
        db,
        action="data_subject_request.export",
        entity_type="data_subject_request",
        entity_id=None,
        actor=current_user,
        exposed=bool(matches),
        detail={"column": payload.column, "match_count": len(matches)},
    )
    return DataSubjectExportResponse(
        column=payload.column,
        value=payload.value,
        match_count=len(matches),
        matches=[
            DataSubjectMatch(
                result_id=m.result_id,
                run_id=m.run_id,
                suite_id=m.suite_id,
                suite_name=m.suite_name,
                check_id=m.check_id,
                check_name=m.check_name,
                created_at=m.created_at,
                matched_in=list(m.matched_in),
                sample_failures=m.sample_failures,
                observed_value=m.observed_value,
            )
            for m in matches
        ],
    )


class DataSubjectErasureResponse(ApiModel):
    column: str
    value: str
    matched_count: int
    erased_count: int


@router.post(
    "/data-subject-requests/erase",
    response_model=DataSubjectErasureResponse,
    summary="Erase a data subject's captured sample data (admin only, GDPR Art 17 / CCPA delete)",
)
def erase_data_subject(
    payload: DataSubjectRequest,
    current_user: Annotated[User, Depends(require_workspace_admin)],
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> DataSubjectErasureResponse:
    """Workspace-wide, on-demand erasure of every captured sample cell naming
    `column` = `value` — surgical (only the matching row/cell), not a blanket purge;
    see `data_subject_requests.erase_matching_results`. Runs synchronously and
    records one `audit_events` row inside the same transaction as the scrub, so a
    failed write leaves nothing behind and an applied one cannot go unrecorded
    (mirrors the ADR 0041 phase-1 mutation pattern).
    """
    summary = data_subject_requests.erase_matching_results(
        db, column=payload.column, value=payload.value
    )
    audit_service.record(
        db,
        action="data_subject_request.erase",
        entity_type="data_subject_request",
        entity_id=None,
        actor=current_user,
        after={
            "column": payload.column,
            "matched_count": len(summary.matched_result_ids),
            "erased_count": summary.erased_count,
        },
    )
    db.commit()
    return DataSubjectErasureResponse(
        column=payload.column,
        value=payload.value,
        matched_count=len(summary.matched_result_ids),
        erased_count=summary.erased_count,
    )

    db_session.flush()

- **Matching is a full scan of the JSONB sample columns**, not an indexed lookup —
  there is no way to index an arbitrary column-name/value match inside a
  schemaless blob. This is an operator-triggered, low-frequency action, not a hot
  path, and is expected to take longer on a workspace with a large results table.
- **Only the shapes the redaction ladder already knows about are covered**:
  `unexpected_index_list` / `partial_unexpected_list` rows, the three comparison
  buckets (`mismatched`, `additional_in_source`, `additional_in_target`), and both
  `observed_value` PII-bearing shapes. A future sample shape needs its own match/
  scrub branch, mirroring how the retention sweep's own shapes are enumerated.
- **Value matching is string equality** (`str(cell) == value`). A numeric or
  differently-formatted cell that is semantically the same value but not the same
  string representation will not match — state that in the response to the
  subject if a match seems to be missing.
- **Neither endpoint reaches `incidents.evidence`.** An incident's stored evidence
  snapshot (see §0) is a separate persisted copy of `observed_value`, not scanned
  or matched by either `export` or `erase` today — an erasure request can leave a
  subject's value sitting in an incident's evidence card even after it is
  confirmed scrubbed from `results`. State this limit to the subject/controller
  if erasure completeness is asked about directly, rather than let the
  `erased_count` response imply full coverage.
- **This does not touch the controller's warehouse** — see §0.

Last reviewed: 2026-09-01.
--- dpia
| `results.sample_failures` | Up to a bounded number of failing rows per check result, as column→value maps | `SAMPLE_FAILURES_RETENTION_DAYS` (default **30**); daily purge sets the column NULL and stamps `sample_failures_purged_at` — the row and its `metric_value` trend survive, the personal data does not | Column-aware **redaction ladder** on every read surface (REST, MCP, alert delivery), d
| `results.observed_value` (list-shaped) | A set-oriented expectation's full observed distinct-value list can reproduce column values | Same purge as `sample_failures` | Same redaction ladder |
| `results.observed_value` (scalar `unparsed_value` cell) | A single unparseable cell value captured for diagnosis | `SAMPLE_FAILURES_RETENTION_DAYS`, same purge as the two rows above | Redaction ladder applies on read |
| `incidents.evidence` (`failing_result.observed_value`) | A stored snapshot of the same kind of literal cell value as the `results.observed_value` rows above, captured once when an incident opens or gets a fresh occurrence | **Not covered by the retention purge** — the snapshot persists for the life of the incident row, independent of the `SAMPLE_FAILURES_RETENTION_DAYS` clock | Redacted throug
| Dry-run / live-probe responses | Real values shown to the check author; **nothing persisted** | Not stored (structurally cannot persist) | Fail-closed suites mask even here; REST dry-run values are shown unredacted by design, a recorded decision |

**Erasure status — state it honestly in your DPIA:** deletion happens on the
retention clock and via entity cascade (deleting a suite/check destroys its
results) **and, on demand, via the [data-subject-rights runbook](data-subject-rights-runbook.md)** — an
Admin-only capability that identifies a subject by a `(column, value)` pair (the
same key the controller's own warehouse row uses; DataQ has no people-table) and
surgically removes only the matching row/cell from `sample_failures` /
`observed_value`, leaving the rest of a result's captured sample — other rows,
other subjects — intact. **This on-demand erasure does not reach `incidents.evidence`**
(the row above) — an incident's stored snapshot survives an on-demand erasure of
the same value from `results`, and only entity cascade (deleting the covering
suite/check/asset) removes it.

def test_export_and_erase_reach_an_incident_evidence_snapshot(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any, as_role: Any
) -> None:
    """#1795: the snapshot is a third persisted copy outside the retention clock."""
    result = _seed_result(
        db_session, sample={"unexpected_index_list": [{"email": "alice@example.com"}]}
    )
    incident = _seed_incident(
        db_session, observed={"observed_value": ["alice@example.com", "x@y.z"]}
    )
    _, headers = as_role("admin")
    payload = {"column": "email", "value": "alice@example.com"}

    body = client.post(
        "/api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/export", json=payload, headers=headers
    ).json()
    assert body["match_count"] == 2 and body["incident_match_count"] == 1
    assert [m["result_id"] for m in body["matches"]] == [str(result.id)]
    hit = body["incident_matches"][0]
    assert hit["incident_id"] == str(incident.id) and hit["status"] == "open"
    assert hit["observed_value"] == {"observed_value": ["alice@example.com", "x@y.z"]}
    access = db_session.scalars(
        select(AuditEvent).where(AuditEvent.action == "data_subject_request.export")
    ).one()
    assert access.detail["incident_match_count"] == 1 and access.detail["match_count"] == 2

    body = client.post(
        "/api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/erase", json=payload, headers=headers
    ).json()
    assert body["matched_count"] == 2 and body["erased_count"] == 2
    assert body["matched_incident_count"] == 1 and body["erased_incident_count"] == 1
    assert body["matched_result_count"] == 1 and body["erased_result_count"] == 1
    db_session.refresh(incident)
    assert incident.evidence is not None
    assert incident.evidence["failing_result"]["observed_value"] == {"observed_value": ["x@y.z"]}
    erase = db_session.scalars(
        select(AuditEvent).where(AuditEvent.action == "data_subject_request.erase")
    ).one()
    assert erase.after["erased_incident_count"] == 1 and erase.after["erased_count"] == 2
